Norton County People: Mr. Snyder, the blacksmith, furnishes an example of what preseverance can do. Last summer he wanted to build used house on his claim, and the ground being too dry to break he hauled fifty-five barrels of water and poured it on the ground, thus securing the requisite moisture. The sod was broken and the house built, which is one of the best in the county. The rooms are large, the ceilings high, well plastered, good floors, well lighted, and as neat and comfortable as any one could wish. A Long-Pending Case Decided.

WASHINGTON, November 23d.—The Commissioner of the General Land Office to-day rendered a final decision in the long-pending case of the rancho Boca De Santas Monica, seven-twelths of which are owned by Senator Jones and R. C. Baker, and the remainder by the original grantees. The novel question presented to Commissioner Williamson was whether he had jurisdiction to dictate a selection of the quantity of land confirmed within the designated exterior boundaries in a case like this, when the owners could not agree upon a selection. He decides that he has jurisdiction, holding that under a decision of the Supreme Court, and upon a proper construction of the Act of July 1, 1864, the making of such selections by the owners of a grant is not a right, but only a privilege given by the generosity of the Government in cases where the confirmees agree upon the selection. He then proceeds to order that the excess of 322 acres shall be thrown off from the eastern portion of the tract by a line commencing in the northeast corner of the judicial possession. The principal part of excess area thus segregated is adjacent to the town of Santa Monica, and the decision is therefore favorable to Jones and Baker.

ONE OF THE PERPETRATORS BURNED AT THE STAKE.

Special to the Picayune.]

TUPELO, Miss., Dec. 20.—Last Saturday night witnessed the most diabolical episode on the history of Mississippi; that of a triple murder and the burning of the victims, after robbing them of the pitiful sum of $27. It appears that two men named Miller called, with the pretext of desiring a night's lodging, at the house of Mr. Brown Riding, who lives in Monroe county, some twenty miles from here. Their request was granted. After retiring, the family having gone to sleep, the men arose and by administering chloform placed them beyond the possibility of molesting their search for booty. After obtaining the money, cotton was spread broadcast over the floor and bed, coal-oil sprinkled thereon, and that ignited; whereupon the men departed in different directions. The neighbors arriving, found it impossible to save anything. After the flames had spent their force the burned remains, unrecognizable, were found with limbs burned off and otherwise disfigured. The family consisted of Mr. Riding, his wife and a two-year old daughter. Search was made for the perpetrators, one of whom was overtaken some six miles from Evergreen. On his person was found nine dollars, Mr. Riding's watch, a suit of clothes and boots. He was returned to the scene of his crime, and there, by seventy-five resolute men, fastened to a stake, splintered with fat pine and permitted to die the death he had so mercilessly meted to his benefactors.

Search is being continued for the other man, who will receive the same punishment if found.

Are the People of Pennsylvania Civilized?
Recently, near the town of Tupelo, in Mississippi, a horrible crime was horribly punished. Two strangers were given shelter for the night by a family, simply out of kindness. The men thus sheltered arose in the night and chloroformed their benefactors robbed them, and then setting the house on fire roasted the insensible inmates alive. The villains were pursued, and one of them caught. He confessed his crime and an infuriated mob burned him alive. Taking this as a text the Norristown (Pa.) Herald preaches a bloody shirt sermon on the barbarism of Mississippi, dragging in the Fort Pillow massacre, the Chisholm murder, the Yazoo homicide and everything it can think of, and it indignantly asks "what kind of courts and juries they must have in a State where the punishment of a man who had acknowledged his guilt of robbery, arson and murder, could not be entrusted to the machinery of the law?"

Last Monday afternoon it was announced that an aged couple living but four miles from Bethlenem, Pennsylvania, had been found brutally murdered, and that a man named Suyder, accused of the deed, was caught by an infuriated mob and hanged to the nearest tree. Later details in the morning papers show that Soyder confessed his crime, and also that the people of the neighborhood approve his lynching. One "respectable "old farmer" told the District Attorney who was criticising the act after it was done that it was all right, and the people did not intend that the lawyers should get any more murderers off on the plea of insanity. In the language of the Norristown Herald we ask "what kind of "courts and juries they must have in a "state where the punishment of a man "who had acknowledged his guilt of "murder could not be intrusted to the "machinery of the law?"

We hope, however, the Herald will not draw too gloomy an inference concerning the barbarism of the State of Pennsylvania from this incident. Of course, a very bad case might be made out, by dwelling on the shameless corruption of its politics, the known purchasability of its legislators, the Pittsburg riot, the Molly Maguire murders and the recent acquittal of a bloody murderer on a trumped up plea of insanity, bringing them all down to this last incident, as the Herald did in discussing the Mississippi tragedy, but the imputation against the majority of the people of the State of Pennsylvania would nevertheless be as unjust as that recently made by the Herald against the people of Mississippi.

THE BIGBY FORK TEAGEDY.
Aberdeen Miss , Dec. 21st, 1880
EDITORS EXAMINER :—On Friday
Aberdeen Miss, Dec. 21st, 1880.

EDITORS EXAMINER:—On Friday night last, in Bighy Fork in this county, a most brutal tragedy was performed by one Alvin McKanna, alias Miller, and his accomplice, one John Gilmore, alias John Howard. The man Alvita McKanna had been in the neighborhood of the place several days, perhaps over a week prior to the act, professing to be a laboring man, and had on one occasion hired to a Mr. Lee for a day or two, and in the meantime had called at several houses to spend the night, at some of which he was permitted to do so. Among other places at which he asked for lodging was the house of William Brown Ridings, about one week before the tragedy occurred, and was denied.

On last Friday evening, Dec. 17th, this man again called at Mr. Ridings' and asked for quarters for the night, and was permitted to stay Mr. Ridings' was a young man whose family consisted of himself, young wife one little infant. About eleven or twelve o'clock at night Mr. Ridings' father, Mr. David Ridings, who lives some three or four hundred yards from his son, discovered his son's house on fire and went to the place, but finding it too far gone to be saved, and seeing no signs of any one in the house, returned home to inform his wife that the family, as he supposed, had gone off on a visit and was safe; after which he returned to the burning house. By that time the building was so far consumed as to discover the charred remains of his son, his wife and child among the ruins. He gave the alarm and next morning the neighbors in large numbers collected at the place and on consultation with the father, it was ascertained that the young man had been to Eureka that day to sell some cotton, and that, together with other money, he had brought home a few dollars in silver; and that he also had a silver watch, neither of which, nor any trace of them could be discovered, although the steel clasp of his pocketbook was found among the ashes. This excited suspicion of foul play and search was immediately instituted for other evidence. Very soon, foot prints were discovered near the place, going into the woods, which were adjudged by those who had known McKanna, to be his tracks. Inquiry was then made as to McKanna's whercabouts when it was ascertained that he had not been seen since the day before in the morning, and at that time was in the woods alone, some mile or mile and a half from the place where the burning had occurred. Very soon a number of resolute young men started out in different directions in search of the supposed murderer. A party overtook and found him Saturday on the William B. Hogan place, in this county, some twelve miles from the scene of the murder, with a new axe, which he said he sent a negro to Cotton Gin to buy for him. He was carried back, and on his way confessed to having been a party to the murder and arson, and took his captors to the place where he had concealed the money, and watch and boots, and other apparel of Mr. Ridings, and everything which he confessed to having gotten was there found and recovered, he giving an account of the whole tragedy about as follows:

He said that he had an accomplice named John Gilmore, alias John Howard; that Gilmore kept himself in the back grounds and was seldom, if ever seen about the scenes of their contemplated operations, but that his, McKanna's, business was to go about the country under the guise of one seeking work, but really hunting victims. Sometimes he would remain in a neighborhood for several days working and visiting about at different houses and making inquiry of the colored and unsuspecting whites as to who had most money, and when he selected the party to be victimized, would report to his partner and a night would be fixed for the accomplishment of the deed. McKanna was to go to the house of a victim to spend the night, and when the family got asleep, if he was in the room with them (as was the case in this instance) he was to apply chloroform to make them sleep soundly, and then give a signal for his accomplice, Gilmore, and they would then rifle the house and rob or commit such other crimes as their cupidity or lusts might suggest.

He says that in this instance he selected Mr. Ridings as his first victim in the neighborhood, and notified Gilmore and placed him in position in the neighborhood of the house so that he could signal him when he should be prepared for him; that after Mr. Ridings and family had gone to sleep, he arose and applied chloroform, and after they were heavily under its influence he went out of the door and whistled, and Gilmore came to him with an axe, with which he struck Mr. Ridings on the head, killing him; that he, Gilmore, violated Mrs. Ridings and tore a ring off her finger; then killed her, with the axe; then took down a can of kerosene oil which was found on the mantle, and poured it on the parties and bedding and floor of the house, and with a match set fire to the building; that as they left the scene they heard the screams of the little burning infant, whom they had even denied the mercy they had extended to the father and mother, of killing it with the pole of the axe before saturating its little garments and bathing its skin with kerosene oil and setting it on fire.

Elsewhere in to-day's Gazette will be found an account, clipped from the Aberdeen Examiner, of a murder committed in Mississippi by a Vigo County murderer who escaped from the prison at Jeffersonville, to which he had been sentenced for life. It proves to be one Piney, at least that is the name he went by here, who, with a confederate named Flowers, shocked this community by the cold-blooded murder of Dr. Armstrong. Instead of being hanged and so put out of the way, he was sentenced by a soft-headed jury to the penitentiary for life. He escaped, of course. If he hadn't, he would in all human probability have been pardoned. Thousands of people, more ar less fools, who mistake soft heads for soft hearts—this class is chiefly made up of women—are never thoroughly aroused to action until they find some miserable scoundrel who has murdered a good man and wrecked the happiness of a family. When they find such an one serving out a sentence in the penitentiary instead of in a warmer place they are always on hand with petitions for pardons and pleas for clemency. With them the only flower in all the universe worth cultivating is the nettle.

But they had not yet done their perfect work with Piney. He anticipated them and escaped, and so completed the weak-kneed Vigo county jury (whose names we have a great mind to republish) by turning loose on the country a skilled thief and practiced assassin. Trained in vice and with a measureless contempt for craven juries who are afraid to do justice, this wild beast, the perfect product of successful crime and outwitted justice, went South, and, with a Vigo county jury in his mind, murdered a family that sheltered and fed him, and then burned down their house about their remains.

If the ghosts of the dead can revisit this earth those of that murdered family ought to haunt the houses of some Vigo county jurors.

But Piney made a mistake in not continuing his murders in Vigo county. He ought to have taken one of our prolific crop ofaddle-pated jurymen.

He went to Mississippi where, thank heaven, they keep and use shot guns and where it has not gone out of fashion to kill those who shed blood.

Piney was caught. There was no sort of doubt about his guilt. In fact they forced a confession. Then they hanged him, and piling faggots around gave his worthless carcass the same fiery sepulture he had accorded the victims of his merciless spite, and a foretaste of horrors he may expect in hell—if there is a hell, and there ought to be one for just such creatures.

These Mississippians into whose hands he fortunately fell only waited to make sure that he was the man.

SOLD INTO SLAVERY.
Three Negroes Sold at Public Auction in Bedford, Va., Under an Old Vagrant Law—Intense Excitement Among the Colored Population—Released by a Writ of Habeas Corpus.

Special Dispatch to The Chicago Tribune.

BEDFORD, Va., Dec. 18.—The recent sale of three negroes at public auction here under an old Vagrant law created the greatest excitement among the negroes, not only in this section, but in other parts of the State. Those of the colored brethren who have heard of the sale have been very uneasy, and the more ignorant of them look upon it as a step towards the reenslavement of the colored race in Virginia. This feeling is intensified by the recent declaration of a negro candidate for office in Essex County, who has come out boldly and announced himself as being in favor of selling both white and colored men who do not pay their capitation taxes. Of course, the matter really does not amount to much. The law under which the negroes were sold is an old one, and is found in several other States, its purpose being to put a stop to vagrancy. The three negroes here were sold for three months, the purchasers being Messrs. John Scott and Daniel Early. Since the sale the negroes in this vicinity became wildly excited over the matter, and employed Mr. H. C. Lowry, a prominent lawyer here, as their counsel. An appeal was at once taken from the decision of the Magistrate, under which the negroes were sold, to Judge Wingfield, of the Circuit Court, but he found upon examination of the law that he could not grant the appeal, the jurisdiction ceasing with the Magistrate's Court in such cases. This decision created still greater consternation among the negroes, who now thought their race doomed, and many of them, with moans or ominous warnings, predicted: "Dey gwine to sell us all into slavery again, shoo." Their counsel then sued out a writ of habeas corpus, which was made returenble before Judge Davis, of the County Court. The Judge now orders the negroes to be discharged on the ground that they did not fall under any of the five heads of vagrancy provided for by the statute, and because the presentation on that charge was not made by the Overseer of the Poor, as required. The three negroes were to-day accordingly given their liberty by their new masters. From having been vagrants, they are now welcome guests in every colored house, being looked upon in the light of martyrs. Nothing has occurred in this section of the State which has so thoroughly worked up the negro race.

The Bloody Regulators.
Wednesday night a party of unknown men fired into a cotton-seed store, kept by Israel Smith, a negro, about five miles miles south of Colfax. At the time there was another man and a boy about 18 years old sleeping in the house with Smith. The boy was shot and killed instantly, the others escaping unhurt. From there there the party went to another seed-store, the property of Messrs. L. E. Torry and S. M. Lacroix, of Colfax, in which W. B. Hopkins was sleeping, and and riddled it with bullets, fortunately not hurting the occupant, but giving him a terrible scare. All those connected with the latter place were were white men.
While the cotton-seed business is most nefarious, still it does not warrant any such murderous work, and those who engaged in this midnight assassination should be hunted down by the strong arm of the law. It is thought the marauding party had no intention of taking life, but this is no excuse for such vandalism. The case is aggravated. No warning had been given. Under the circumstances, it would have been most harsh to call out the victim and burn his house, allowing him to go with his life, but to come unawares and shoot a man in the dark is horrible. This act certainly must have been committed by irresponsible parties, for no sane man, with the interest of the country at heart, and the good of himself and neighbors in view, could have been led into committing such an attrocious barbarism.

A coal oil lamp nearly caused the destruction of the Creole Store together with our postoffice one night last week. The oil within the lamp had ignited, creating a large flame which ascended to the ceiling above, causing it to burn. Fortunately, Mr. Toney Madere had not retired for the night, but on entering the store discovered the situation at a glance, siezed the burning lamp, threw it into the street, and returning to the store, extinguished the flame before material damage was done. Had this gentleman been asleep the destruction of the building would have been inevitable. We regret that our handsome young friend received some slight burns on the hands.—[St. Charles Herald.

A MELANCHOLY CASE OF HYDROPHOBIA.—Mr. R. H. Wade, of Marthaville, informed us, a few days ago, of a singular case of this dreadful malady. The victim is a boy 17 years old, named Thomas Dew, living within two miles of that town. It appears he was bitten by a dog, showing no signs of being rabid, over two years ago. The wound was healed, and nothing more was thought about it. Lately, however, the terrible malady has plainly manifested itself, and the unfortunate youth gets furious when his father or mother comes in his presence. When the paroxisms are over, he whittles and sings as formerly. Though very frail, it takes two strong men to hold him while the fit is on. Surely, better every dog in the State were dead than that one case of this kind should occur.—[Natchitoches Vindicator.

A DISTARDLY ATTEMPT.—An attempt at highway robbery was perpetrated upon a worthy, quiet and peaceable citizen of this town. On last Thursday night as Mr. Raudner was returning from Evergreen he was met and accosted by two persons near Dr. Forest’s residence on the outskirts of Mansura. Their attitude and their demonstration were of such a nature as to leave no doubt in the mind of Mr. Raudner that there was mischief brewing. A peaceable citizen coming from a neighboring town is met upon the highway with the question, "Where are you going and have you money?" Our astonished citizen responded that he had no money and was going to Marksville. These unknown persons acquainted with the fact that he was an industrious workman, supposed to have or to control money, at once determined to execute a hellish deed—to commit highway robbery in our parish. By persuasion and by threats Mr. Raudner succeeded in reaching the residence of Dr. Forest where he found protection against the robbers who were at the gate.—[Marksville Bulletin.

Murderous Incendiaries.
There are a set of cowardy cut-throats some eight or ten miles southeast of Colfax, on Bayou Philip or Bayou Darro, who richly deserves a term in the penitentiary or justice at the end of a limb. Last Thursday night, about ten o'clock, they set fire to a store owned by two colored men, Israel Smith and Hansom Brisco, and burned it to the ground. The store had goods in it amounting to nearly $800, and the building was worth about $100 more. While the store was in flames several volleys were fired into it. No one was in it at the time, the occupants being at a house several hundred yards away, and too frightened to venture near. This party is evidently the same set who killed a young negro man in the same store early in the fall, by shooting through the walls. Measures should be taken to break up this nest of outlaws, and we hope to see active operations to do so commenced at once. These negroes are entitled to protection, and our community cannot prosper with such a set of cut-throats in it. Israel Smith, one of the store proprietors, says he has no clue as to whether the party consisted of white or black men.

The animus of this act probably was to strike a blow at the "seed cotton" traffic. But it is rather late in the day for that; beside, it is a poor beginning to make on a couple of timid negroes, who are only following the lead of a dozen white men who have done the same business all the past fall.
